> **Code:** [common correlated effects](index.qmd#sec-cce) for the
> estimates, [the exponent α](index.qmd#sec-csd-exponent) for the routing
> that sends a panel here. Related note:
> [cross-sectional dependence](theory-cross-sectional-dependence.qmd).

## Why the method exists

Regress log house prices on log income state by state and average the 49
slopes: 0.30. Add two cross-state averages to each regression and do it
again: 1.14 [@holly2010; @croissant2019, pp. 197–199]. Nothing about the
data changed. What changed is that the second regression controls for a
national force, interest rates and credit conditions, that moves both prices
and incomes in every state, each to its own degree.

The obvious control is a year effect: a dummy for each year, which removes
whatever is common to all states in that year. It fails here for one
reason. A year effect removes the force only if every state feels it by the
same amount. When states differ in how hard the force hits, the part of it
that differs stays in the error, correlated with income, and the slope is
biased. Not inefficient: biased, and no standard-error correction helps
[cross-sectional dependence](theory-cross-sectional-dependence.qmd). CCE is
the fix for that case, and this note says why it works and when it does not.

## 1. The model, and why year effects fail

State *i* in year *t* follows

$$
y_{it} = \alpha_i + \beta_i x_{it} + u_{it}, \qquad
u_{it} = \lambda_i f_t + \varepsilon_{it},
$$

where $f_t$ is the unobserved **common factor**, the national force, and
$\lambda_i$ is state *i*'s **loading** on it, how hard the force hits that
state. The factor is also in the regressor:

$$
x_{it} = a_i + \gamma_i f_t + v_{it}.
$$

Income and the error share $f_t$, so each state's OLS slope picks up the
factor's effect on prices and attributes it to income. That is the leak.

A year effect subtracts the cross-state mean from every variable in every
year. In the error that leaves $(\lambda_i - \bar\lambda) f_t$: the factor
survives in proportion to how far each state's loading sits from the
average. Two-way fixed effects is a factor model with every loading equal to
one, and it removes the factor only in that case. With heterogeneous
loadings the bias stays, and α near 1 is exactly the panel where loadings
are heterogeneous enough to matter [@pesaran2015, p. 754].

## 2. Why averages work

Average the price equation over the N states in year *t*:

$$
\bar y_t = \bar\alpha + \bar\beta \bar x_t + \bar\lambda f_t
  + \bar\varepsilon_t + o_p(1),
$$

and the income equation likewise, $\bar x_t = \bar a + \bar\gamma f_t +
\bar v_t$. As N grows the idiosyncratic averages $\bar\varepsilon_t$ and
$\bar v_t$ vanish, and the two averages are left as two linear functions of
one unknown, $f_t$. Solve for it:

$$
f_t \approx \frac{\bar y_t - \bar\alpha - \bar\beta \bar x_t}{\bar\lambda}.
$$

The unobserved factor is, for large N, a known combination of the observed
averages. So put the averages themselves into each state's regression,

$$
y_{it} = \alpha_i + \beta_i x_{it} + c_i \bar y_t + d_i \bar x_t + e_{it},
$$

and let each state choose its own $c_i$ and $d_i$. Whatever $\lambda_i$ is,
the pair $(c_i, d_i)$ can absorb $\lambda_i f_t$, because $f_t$ lies in the
space the averages span. The factor is controlled for without being
estimated, and without assuming anything about its time path. That is the
whole of @pesaran2006, and it survives factors that wander like random walks
[@kapetanios2011], which is why the method is safe on price *levels*.

With *m* factors and *k* regressors there are $k + 1$ averages, and they
span the factors only if $m \le k + 1$ and the $(k+1) \times m$ matrix of
average loadings has full column rank: the **rank condition**
[@pesaran2006]. One regressor buys at most two factors.

## 3. CCEMG and CCEP

Two ways to turn 49 augmented regressions into one slope
[@pesaran2015, pp. 767–768].

**CCEMG**, mean group, runs the augmented regression state by state and
averages the slopes:

$$
\hat\beta_{\text{CCEMG}} = \frac1N \sum_{i=1}^N \hat\beta_i, \qquad
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}} = \frac{1}{N(N-1)} \sum_{i=1}^N
  (\hat\beta_i - \hat\beta_{\text{CCEMG}})^2 .
$$

The variance is the dispersion of the 49 slopes: no assumption about the
errors within a state enters it, and it is honest about heterogeneous
slopes, which is why the stripchart in the
[step](index.qmd#sec-cce) is the estimate's own picture.

**CCEP**, pooled, imposes one slope on every state while keeping the
state-specific $\alpha_i$, $c_i$ and $d_i$, and estimates it by least
squares on the augmented data. Its variance is a sandwich that allows the
true slopes to differ across states by random amounts [@croissant2019,
sec. 8.3.2.2]. Under one common slope CCEP is the more efficient of the two.
When the slopes differ, both estimate their mean, and CCEMG does so without
weighting states by how much their income varies.

Read them together. CCEMG 1.14 and CCEP 1.20, each with a standard error of
0.2, are one number: the spread in the state slopes is noise around a common
value, and the pooled estimate can be reported [@croissant2019, p. 199].
Had they been far apart, the slopes would be genuinely heterogeneous and
CCEMG would be the one to report.

## 4. What CCE does not fix

- **Factors that average out.** If the loadings on a factor average to
  zero across states, $\bar\lambda = 0$, the averages do not carry it and
  the rank condition fails. @pesaran2006 shows the estimators can survive
  this when the loadings are independent of the regressors' loadings, but
  nothing in the output says whether that holds.
- **More factors than averages.** With one regressor and three factors the
  averages span two of them. The remedy is more averages, of variables that
  load on the missing factors even if they are not in the regression, which
  `plm::pcce` does not provide. The exponent on the CCE residuals is the
  check: if it is still near 1, a factor was missed
  ([the exponent α](index.qmd#sec-csd-exponent)).
- **A lagged dependent variable.** With $y_{i,t-1}$ on the right, the
  augmented regression is biased at short T, and @chudik2015 add lags of the
  averages to repair it. Dynamic panels are a later part of
  [time dependence](../04-time/index.qmd).
- **Weak dependence.** When α is near ½ the averages carry nothing and CCE
  changes nothing. The dependence that remains is local, and a spatial
  model is the tool ([spatial dependence](../03-spatial/index.qmd)).
- **Interactive fixed effects** [@bai2009] estimate the factors and
  loadings by principal components instead of proxying them. They need the
  number of factors chosen in advance and more of T; CCE needs neither,
  which is why this book uses CCE first.

## 5. If / then

| If | Then |
|---|---|
| α ≈ 1, or CD rejects on the raw series | Year effects are not enough. CCE [@pesaran2006]. |
| CCEMG and CCEP agree within a standard error | One common slope. Report CCEP, keep CCEMG as the check [@croissant2019, p. 199]. |
| CCEMG and CCEP differ by more than that | Heterogeneous slopes. Report CCEMG; its variance is the dispersion of the slopes. |
| α on the CCE residuals is still near 1 | A factor was missed: more factors than averages. State it as a limitation. |
| The series wander | CCE still holds [@kapetanios2011]. Test the residuals for a unit root ([tests that allow a common factor](../04-time/index.qmd#sec-ur-second-gen)). |
| A lagged outcome is a regressor | Short-T bias. Lags of the averages [@chudik2015], not plain CCE. |

## 6. Open

- **The number of factors is never tested here.** The rank condition is
  assumed, and the only check is the exponent on the residuals, which can
  say that something was missed but not what.
- **Rank-condition failure.** The conditions under which CCE survives it
  are in @pesaran2006 and are not verified for the house-price panel.
- **Heterogeneous slopes in CCEP.** The sandwich variance assumes the slope
  deviations are random and independent of the regressors; the step does
  not test it.
